routes.description: Establish the relevant historical data, defend their evidential reliability, and show that divine resurrection explains them more adequately than the principal skeptical alternatives within an independently supported theistic context.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the core data are sufficiently established, the resurrection is not excluded by an improperly fixed prior or evidential threshold, and its comparative explanatory advantages support treating it as the best historical explanation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the established historical data to the conclusion that Jesus's resurrection is their best explanation.

centralBridges.description: Establish the burial, empty tomb, postmortem experiences, and transformed disciple belief as historical data requiring explanation.
Show that fabrication, hallucination, and legendary development lack sufficient explanatory scope or power relative to resurrection.
Justify assessing resurrection within a theistic context in which divine action is not antecedently prohibitive.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend best-explanation and probability reasoning as an appropriate form of historical proof without requiring mathematical certainty.
Clarify how cumulative arguments, personal experience, and practical stakes relate to, but do not replace, the historical case.

routes.description: Prevent the resurrection conclusion by challenging the adequacy and reliability of the proposed historical data, defending naturalistic or source-critical alternatives, and requiring evidential support proportionate to the supernatural claim and its asserted divine context.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if uncertainty in the underlying reports, plausible skeptical alternatives, or unresolved prior-probability and evidence-expectation concerns keep resurrection from being warranted as the best explanation.

motionBridge.description: Show that skeptical alternatives and evidential uncertainty prevent the resurrection from being established as the best explanation.

centralBridges.description: Contest whether appearance reports, the empty tomb, and related claims are reliable and sufficiently established historical data.
Preserve sincere error, hallucination, legendary development, or combined naturalistic accounts as live explanatory alternatives.
Show that the resurrection's prior improbability and the expected evidence under divine authorship require more than ordinary-quality historical support.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether public counterevidence can override experiential warrant and whether the resurrection claim has a meaningful falsification condition.
Relate the claim's exceptional historical and religious consequence to the degree of evidential caution appropriate before accepting it.

sections.title: Historical Proof, Evidential Standards, and Prior Probability
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether ordinary best-explanation reasoning can establish a supernatural event, how prior probability enters the comparison, and whether a theistic context or the claim's extraordinary character changes the evidential burden.

sections.title: Core Historical Data and Source Reliability
sections.rationale: The comparative inference depends on whether burial, the empty tomb, postmortem experiences, and transformed belief are adequately supported by early and independent sources rather than uncertain or developing reports.

sections.title: Fabrication, Hallucination, and Legendary Development
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether sincere error, grief-related experiences, deliberate invention, legendary growth, or combinations of naturalistic hypotheses can explain the proposed data without invoking resurrection.

sections.title: Experiential Warrant, Falsification, and Practical Stakes
sections.rationale: This issue clarifies the relationship between personal religious experience and public historical evidence, identifies potential defeaters, and determines what role practical consequences may have alongside the historical inference.

routes.description: Establish that the relevant conception of God remains coherent when maximal attributes are defined through genuine logical possibilities, divine knowledge is reconciled with freedom, and apparent bodily, temporal, or infinite-task limitations are distinguished from genuine deficits of power.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supplies a mutually consistent account of maximal power, knowledge, goodness, embodiment, and temporality that answers the quantitative-infinity objection and preserves a recognizable burden-relevant conception of theism.

motionBridge.description: Show that the divine attributes relevant to the motion admit a jointly coherent interpretation without requiring impossible quantitative magnitudes.

centralBridges.description: Define maximal power by the range of logically possible actions and explain why unrestricted ability need not be an impossible quantitative infinity.
Specify the extent of divine knowledge consistently with divine freedom and explain how any restriction relates to the relevant theistic conception.
Show that apparent limitations arising from embodiment, temporality, or supertasks concern incoherent descriptions or category distinctions rather than absent genuine powers.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect the defended attribute set to historically or explanatorily relevant theism rather than assuming that every maximal quantitative formulation is mandatory.
Explain how evaluative knowledge and freedom from conflicting desires can make perfect goodness compatible with the defended account of omnipotence.

routes.description: Establish that the stipulated maximal conception of God requires impossible infinite quantities of power, knowledge, or intelligence, and show that proposed restrictions or reinterpretations either fail to remove those infinities or generate further conflicts among divine attributes and doctrines.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if maximal theism cannot avoid impossible non-extensive infinities without relinquishing motion-relevant attributes, or if its proposed repairs produce contradictions involving freedom, timelessness, embodiment, action, or completed infinite processes.

motionBridge.description: Show that the motion-relevant maximal divine attributes require impossible magnitudes or otherwise cannot be jointly instantiated coherently.

centralBridges.description: Establish that all-powerfulness and comprehensive cognition require unbounded or infinite quantities rather than merely a finite list of action kinds or truths.
Show that limiting foreknowledge or redescribing actions does not eliminate the infinite power, information, or intelligence implicated by the remaining attributes.
Demonstrate that proposed repairs involving timelessness, bodilessness, or temporal-event analysis conflict with other theistic commitments or fail on their own terms.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish allegedly possible extensive infinities from the impossible quantitative infinities attributed to divine power and cognition.
Test abstract coherence defenses against incarnation, changing divine intentions, and completed infinite-action cases that expose their material implications.

sections.title: Maximal power and quantitative infinity
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether omnipotence can be understood as a coherent range of abilities or necessarily entails an impossible infinite magnitude of power.

sections.title: Divine knowledge, freedom, and the relevant theistic conception
sections.rationale: The scope of divine knowledge determines whether omniscience conflicts with freedom and whether restricting foreknowledge preserves the conception of theism placed in issue.

sections.title: Actual infinity, divisibility, and supertasks
sections.rationale: Spatial division and the lamp supertask test the parties' competing accounts of actual infinity, temporally extended action, and the implications of unrestricted divine agency.

sections.title: Bodilessness, incarnation, and divine action
sections.rationale: The relationship between necessary bodilessness and incarnation determines whether bodily inabilities are merely logical exclusions or internal tensions within the relevant theology.

sections.title: Timelessness, change, and foreknowledge
sections.rationale: Timelessness offers a possible reconciliation of knowledge and control of the future, while divine changes of intention test whether that reconciliation is internally consistent.

routes.description: Establish an objective standard under which unusual historical beliefs can be reasonable, show that the resurrection reports constitute admissible testimony, and argue that the relevant facts, expected evidence, and comparative explanations leave divine resurrection as a reasonable account.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if historical testimony can warrant an unusual event, the cited resurrection materials support sincere postmortem-experience claims, ordinary alternatives do not explain the relevant evidence equally well, and divine agency remains compatible with the applicable background knowledge and expected evidence.

motionBridge.description: Connect the historical and explanatory case to the conclusion that believing Jesus rose can be reasonable without requiring personal conviction or certainty.

centralBridges.description: Supply a determinate standard for reasonable belief in an unusual historical event based on established facts, expected evidence, and comparative explanations.
Establish that the historical sources provide evidentially relevant testimony to sincere experiences and proclamations associated with Jesus after his death.
Show why legend, deception, error, hallucination, or transmission accounts do not explain the relevant testimonial and historical claims as adequately as resurrection.
Preserve divine resurrection as an available explanation by defending the possibility of divine agency and rejecting a presumption that natural regularity excludes exceptions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why testimony and historical inquiry can convey knowledge even when direct physical inspection or experimental replication is unavailable.
Clarify the evidential role of costly witness commitment and identify what kinds of contrary historical evidence could undermine the resurrection case.

routes.description: Distinguish the reasonableness of accepting resurrection from the event's truth, require evidence proportioned to background knowledge and the claim's unusual character, and argue that inaccessible testimony without adequate corroboration does not warrant accepting resurrection over ordinary human error.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the available ancient reports cannot be sufficiently verified or corroborated, ordinary error or transmission remains more consistent with established experience, supernatural agency lacks independent warrant, and the evidence falls short of what accepting this unusual historical claim reasonably requires.

motionBridge.description: Connect the evidential deficiencies to the conclusion that accepting the resurrection is unreasonable without undertaking to prove that it did not occur.

centralBridges.description: Ground reasonable acceptance in established knowledge about reality and require stronger support when testimony conflicts with well-supported background experience.
Show that ancient testimonial chains cannot be adequately identified, questioned, reconciled, or physically corroborated for the resurrection conclusion.
Maintain that mistake, deception, interpretive error, or distorted transmission remains a more warranted account of resurrection reports than a supernatural event.
Require independent demonstration of supernatural possibility before divine action can function as a warranted explanation of the historical reports.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Compare the surviving record with the stronger and more accessible evidence that a capable relational deity or a confirmed resurrection phenomenon could provide.
Separate evidence that witnesses sincerely held a belief from evidence that their interpretation of the reported experience was accurate.

sections.title: Reasonableness Standards and Debate Burdens
sections.rationale: The motion turns on the threshold for justified acceptance rather than solely on whether the event occurred, making the competing definitions of reasonableness, conviction, and burden foundational to every later issue.

sections.title: Historical Testimony and Source Reliability
sections.rationale: The resurrection case depends principally on ancient reports, so the evidential status of testimony, the accessibility and reliability of the sources, and the legitimacy of historical inference form a major shared issue.

sections.title: Resurrection and Ordinary Alternative Explanations
sections.rationale: The motion requires comparing resurrection with error, deception, legend, hallucination, misidentification, and transmission accounts rather than assessing the reports without explanatory alternatives.

sections.title: Background Knowledge, Natural Regularity, and Divine Agency
sections.rationale: Whether resurrection is a live explanatory possibility depends on the role of established natural regularities, the warranted scope of scientific inquiry, and any independent basis for supernatural or divine agency.

sections.title: Expected Evidence, Corroboration, and Falsifiability
sections.rationale: The presence or absence of physical corroboration, accessible witnesses, modern confirmation, divine disclosure, and potential counterevidence bears directly on what evidence should be expected if the claim were true.

sections.title: Witness Sincerity and Evidential Sufficiency
sections.rationale: Costly commitment and multiple attestations may bear on sincerity, while the dispute over sufficient evidence determines whether sincerity and accumulated testimony can support the further resurrection inference.

routes.description: Establish that determinism and indeterminism both fail to provide the conscious authorship and same-circumstances alternatives integral to free will, and that practical capacities or accountability conventions do not supply what is missing.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if unauthored causes, constitutive luck, and unconscious processes defeat ultimate authorship while randomness supplies no control, leaving compatibilist competence and social regulation unable to establish free will in the disputed sense.

motionBridge.description: Show that neither causal determination nor indeterminacy permits the authorship and alternative possibilities required for free will and ultimate moral responsibility.

centralBridges.description: Establish that preserving useful capacities under the name free will omits the first-person authorship and actual ability to have done otherwise that motivate the dispute.
Show that genes, environment, prior brain states, and unconscious processes produce character and choice without being authored by the agent.
Distinguish useful accountability and behavioral regulation from genuine authorship or ultimate moral responsibility for causally produced conduct.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that tracing conduct to earlier choices only moves the authorship problem backward, while microscopic contingencies expose pervasive causal luck.
Show that randomness adds no ownership and that sufficiently informative advance prediction would expose rather than create conscious authorship.

routes.description: Establish that freedom worth preserving is the graded, naturalistic competence to deliberate, respond to reasons, exercise self-control, and undertake obligations, none of which requires exemption from deterministic causation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if reasons-responsive control supports meaningful agency and calibrated responsibility, while demands for absolute self-creation, exact-replay alternatives, or indeterministic choice are shown unnecessary to the distinctions and practices free will must preserve.

motionBridge.description: Show that reasons-responsive agency supplies a determinism-compatible form of freedom sufficient for meaningful control and moral responsibility.

centralBridges.description: Define free agency through functioning capacities for reflection, ordered desire, attention, self-control, learning, and responsiveness to reasons.
Show that genuine control and temporally extended authorship do not require control of every background condition or awareness of every implementing microprocess.
Ground responsibility in graded competence, obligations, justified reliance, and stable consequentialist practices rather than absolute metaphysical desert.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain ability to do otherwise through robust competencies and relevantly similar circumstances rather than atom-for-atom replay of the universe.
Show that quantum indeterminacy adds no morally relevant freedom unavailable from deterministic deliberation, control, and practical randomness.

sections.title: The Concept and Stakes of Free Will
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether naturalistic conceptual revision preserves the phenomenon at stake or changes the subject by omitting authorship and same-circumstances alternatives.

sections.title: Reasons-Responsive Competence and Bounded Control
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether deliberation, self-control, obligations, and responsiveness to reasons constitute genuine agency despite dependence on uncontrolled causal conditions.

sections.title: Authorship, Constitutive Luck, and Neural Causation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether genes, environment, prior brain states, anomalous lapses, and unconscious implementation defeat authorship or remain compatible with temporally extended self-governance.

sections.title: Alternative Possibilities, Replay, and Randomness
sections.rationale: This issue compares exact-replay ability with competence across relevantly similar circumstances and tests whether deterministic chaos or indeterminacy contributes anything morally significant.

sections.title: Moral Responsibility, Accountability, and Social Practice
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether causal explanation universally exculpates or whether graded competence, reliance, deterrence, rehabilitation, and stable institutions sustain responsibility without absolute authorship.

moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn follows the explicit handoff to Dennett and consistently presents his compatibilist position in the first person.

routes.description: Establish that actual psychophysical harmony is a distinctive, value-producing arrangement whose comparative likelihood is materially greater given a perfectly good creator than given naturalism, including naturalistic identity theories that retain an epistemic gap.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if harmony remains a legitimate evidential datum, relevant alternatives make it comparatively unexpected on naturalism, divine goodness supplies a reason to expect it on theism, and the likelihood comparison remains warranted against reductive and probabilistic objections.

motionBridge.description: Show that psychophysical harmony raises the comparative evidential standing of God over naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Specify the normative, functional, and value-producing fit that constitutes the relevant harmony datum.
Establish a relevant range of epistemically available disharmonious mappings that naturalism does not preferentially predict.
Connect perfect divine goodness and power to reasons for realizing consciousness-involving goods through harmonious arrangements.
Defend meaningful comparative likelihood ordering despite identity claims, sparse backgrounds, and unavailable precise measures.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why evolutionary history does not independently account for the experience-to-function alignment under examination.
Show why the evidential datum may be comparative and value-producing without requiring maximal harmony in every instance.

routes.description: Establish that psychophysical harmony does not supply the claimed comparative evidence for God because reductive identity naturalism removes an independent mapping to explain, restricts the alleged alternatives, and undermines ungrounded likelihood assignments over epistemic possibilities.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if identity naturalism makes the harmony datum non-independent or expected, the proposed disharmonious alternatives lack adequate modal support, and no principled comparative likelihood favors theism once complete theories, simplicity, and fit are considered.

motionBridge.description: Show that psychophysical harmony does not shift the evidential comparison from naturalism toward God.

centralBridges.description: Establish that phenomenal and physical descriptions may concern identical events rather than a contingent correlation requiring selection.
Defend sufficiently strong constraints on epistemic possibility to exclude or limit the proposed inverted and recombined alternatives.
Require a principled basis for comparative likelihoods across the relevant psychophysical laws or complete theories.
Compare explanatory commitments, simplicity, and fit without assuming that sparse-background Bayesian quantities are available.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify whether a generic necessary pain-avoidance connection can permit exceptional cases without surrendering the central constraint.
Account for reductive materialism as a theory of consciousness that can be combined with either naturalism or theism.

sections.title: The Harmony Datum and Its Value-Producing Character
sections.rationale: This issue determines what must be explained or compared: the alignment among phenomenal character, normative significance, functional role, and consciousness-involving goods, including whether imperfection prevents that alignment from constituting a distinctive datum.

sections.title: Comparative Expectation on Theism and Naturalism
sections.rationale: The motion turns on whether harmonious psychophysical arrangements are comparatively expected given divine goodness and comparatively unexpected given naturalism, including whether evolutionary processes account for the observed alignment.

sections.title: Identity, Reduction, and the Epistemic Gap
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether identity naturalism dissolves an independent psychophysical correlation or whether an epistemic gap leaves the relevant likelihood comparison intact despite necessary phenomenal-physical identities.

sections.title: Conceivability and the Modal Space of Psychophysical Alternatives
sections.rationale: The improbability claim depends on whether inverted, zombie, exceptional, and recombined scenarios are legitimate epistemic alternatives, while the opposing route requires principled constraints capable of excluding or limiting them.

sections.title: Likelihood Grounding and Complete-Theory Comparison
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether ordinal evidential comparisons can remain justified without precise probabilities or a privileged measure, and whether simplicity, fit, and explanatory commitments instead supply the proper framework for comparing the hypotheses.

routes.description: Establish that theism offers a better overall explanation by supplying a non-causal ground for contingent reality, a principled ultimate explanatory terminus, and an epistemically coherent account of religious experience and diversity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the theistic resources jointly provide material explanatory advantages over naturalistic alternatives while meeting challenges concerning brute necessity, experiential unreliability, divine communication, and religious disagreement.

motionBridge.description: Show that theism's combined treatment of contingent reality and religious experience makes it the better overall explanation relative to naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Require a non-causal and non-necessitating explanation of the contingent total causal history and identify divine free grounding as the relevant resource.
Provide a principled ultimate terminus whose essence entails existence and explain why a theistic candidate has comparative explanatory relevance.
Justify giving context-sensitive evidential weight to religious experience, testimony, and cultivated religious practices.
Account for ambiguity and religious diversity without requiring that divine communication chiefly produce uniform and detailed theology.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify grounding as the relation by which divine creative activity could unify and explain created causal reality.
Distinguish degrees of experiential and testimonial reliability while preserving qualified trust amid disagreement.

routes.description: Establish that naturalism can match or exceed theism's explanatory coverage without adding God by offering naturalistic foundations for contingent history and explaining religious phenomena through calibrated cognition, social processes, and nonintentional causes.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic accounts cover the principal explanatory domains without a uniquely theistic resource and if the proposed theistic stopping points and experiential expectations do not establish an overall comparative advantage.

motionBridge.description: Show that adding God does not improve the overall explanation once naturalistic alternatives and the comparative costs of theistic explanations are included.

centralBridges.description: Supply a naturalistic structure in which necessary initial reality and indeterministic evolution explain the occurrence of a contingent history.
Require equal scrutiny of naturalistic and theistic ultimate necessities and deny an asymmetry based only on naming a developed divine essence.
Explain why religious experience must be calibrated for ordinary unreliability, cognitive mechanisms, and the relevant comparison class.
Relate ambiguity, unsuccessful visionaries, and enduring religious diversity to the expectations of intentional divine communication and naturalistic causation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Compare explanatory coverage and simplicity across complete worldviews without double-counting a disputed explanatory deficiency.
Preserve live naturalistic ultimate candidates where present knowledge of cosmic origins does not determine their essential structure.

sections.title: Standards for Comparing Complete Worldviews
sections.rationale: This issue fixes how explanatory coverage, simplicity, uncertainty, and reasonable disagreement bear on the motion, and therefore governs how the more specific causal and experiential disputes contribute to an overall comparison.

sections.title: Grounding and the Explanation of Contingent Causal History
sections.rationale: The debate's principal metaphysical clash concerns whether contingent causal history requires a non-causal, non-necessitating ground or can be explained through necessary natural conditions with indeterministic evolution.

sections.title: Necessary Existence and Explanatory Termination
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether theism supplies a principled ultimate explanatory terminus unavailable to naturalism, or whether divine and natural foundations face symmetrical demands concerning necessity, essence, and bruteness.

sections.title: Epistemic Weight and Naturalistic Calibration of Religious Experience
sections.rationale: Religious experience is a distinct proposed source of comparative support whose force depends on default trust, testimonial and first-person justification, learned practices, cognitive mechanisms, and calibrated unreliability.

sections.title: Divine Communication, Visionaries, and Religious Diversity
sections.rationale: The distribution, ambiguity, and durability of divergent traditions test whether religious phenomena fit intentional divine relationship or nonintentional natural and sociological processes within the competing worldviews.

routes.description: Establish that contingent reality calls for an explanation outside the totality of contingent things and that an automatically actual foundation is a better stopping point than brute contingency.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its explanatory principle legitimately applies to contingent reality as a whole, excludes a contingent explanans from completing the explanation, and supports a noncontingent foundation without requiring an indefensible account of necessity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the explanatory facts about contingent reality provide rational support for moving to an automatically actual or necessary foundation.

centralBridges.description: Specify and defend the principle that contingent things have an explanation and that their collective explanation cannot be one of the contingent things explained.
Justify extending ordinary explanatory and abductive reasoning to reality's foundational structure rather than exempting the totality from inquiry.
Explain why automatic actuality or noncontingency removes the distinctive explanatory demand generated by actuality that could have failed.
Provide a coherent route from explanatory fundamentality to an appropriate kind of necessity, including the relation between logical necessity and a concrete foundation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish relevant strengths of necessity so the foundational conclusion does not depend on epistemic certainty or an unnecessarily strong modal formulation.
Account for why apparent conceivability of a foundationless or godless world need not establish genuine metaphysical possibility.

routes.description: Establish that explanatory reasoning within contingent reality does not warrant a necessary foundation, because an ultimate brute or independent foundation may remain contingent and necessity adds no decisive explanation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if global explanatory demands remain unsupported or if fundamentality, independence, and bruteness can be separated from modal necessity, leaving a contingent universe or other brute foundation as a live endpoint.

motionBridge.description: Show that the move from contingent reality or an unexplained foundation to a necessary or automatically actual foundation is not warranted.

centralBridges.description: Require justification for applying causal and explanatory intuitions formed within reality to spacetime, total reality, or its ultimate boundary.
Show why labeling a foundation necessary does not explain its actuality and may reverse or circularize the proposed explanatory direction.
Separate explanatory independence and absence of a further explanation from existence in every possible world.
Require a bridge from necessary logical or abstract truths to the necessary existence of a concrete, causally capable foundation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish whether comparable bruteness can be assigned to the universe or another contingent foundation without additional explanatory cost.
Test appeals to hidden contradiction and conceivability by clarifying when undiscovered identities or inferential consequences determine genuine contradiction.

sections.title: The explanatory principle and its application to total contingent reality
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether contingent reality generates an explanatory burden and whether the explanation must lie outside the collection of contingent things rather than terminate within it.

sections.title: Global explanatory inference versus a brute foundation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether explanatory practices legitimately extend to ultimate reality and whether a brute universe or other foundation remains an adequate alternative endpoint.

sections.title: The explanatory role of automatic actuality and necessity
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether noncontingency answers the relevant demand for explanation or merely redescribes an unexplained foundation while introducing circularity about supremacy and necessity.

sections.title: Fundamentality, independence, and modal necessity
sections.rationale: This issue addresses the key transition from being ultimate, independent, or without further explanation to being unable not to exist across the relevant range of possibilities.

sections.title: Logic, conceivability, and a concrete necessary foundation
sections.rationale: This issue covers whether necessary logical structure supports a concrete foundation and whether conceivability, hidden contradictions, or abstract-truth commitments establish or undermine that connection.

routes.description: Establish that intelligible thought and inquiry depend on interconnected logical, epistemic, metaphysical, inductive, and ethical preconditions, and that the Orthodox Christian God supplies their coherent and necessary ground.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects unavoidable preconditions of discourse and experience to a specifically Orthodox metaphysical account, explains why non-theistic alternatives cannot supply the same unified justification, and defends the transcendental method used to establish that dependence.

motionBridge.description: Show that the preconditions of intelligibility cannot be coherently justified unless the Orthodox Christian God is presupposed.

centralBridges.description: Establish that paradigm-level presuppositions require transcendental assessment and that unavoidable circularity at this level does not reduce the case to an ordinary explanatory inference.
Show that attempts to deny fundamental logical norms still depend on logical regularities required for meaningful language, predication, and argument.
Connect scientific induction and natural regularity to a meta-level justification grounded in divine providence rather than merely assuming isolated regularities.
Explain how creation, divine archetypes, the logoi, and the essence-energies distinction ground shared intelligible content while preserving real distinctions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish a non-Christian's practical use of reason from the worldview-level justification claimed to make that use coherent.
Relate the claimed logical and mathematical preconditions to the structures operative in actual human experience despite conceivable alternative formal systems.

routes.description: Show that the proposed transcendental reasoning does not establish that logic, induction, knowledge, ethics, or abstract content uniquely require the Orthodox Christian God, because the necessity inference and proposed grounding remain contestable.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it identifies a coherent non-Orthodox understanding of the relevant preconditions or shows that the affirmative method, necessity claims, induction account, and divine-conceptualist explanation do not establish the asserted exclusive dependence.

motionBridge.description: Show that the named preconditions can be understood without presupposing the Orthodox Christian God or that their alleged dependence has not been established.

centralBridges.description: Require a demonstrated connection between Orthodox belief and coherent thought rather than inferring necessity from the presence of worldview assumptions.
Show that challenges to classical logical laws can remain intelligible and that reductio does not establish universal non-contradiction against contradiction-tolerant positions.
Show that invoking providence does not nontrivially justify particular inductive expectations and may leave the underlying epistemic burden unchanged.
Develop non-theistic access to abstract objects and moral truths while testing whether divine thought explains shared abstract content without recreating the same distinction.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify whether the affirmative case is a transcendental proof, a paradigm-coherence comparison, or an explanatory inference, and identify the completion standard for that form.
Use alternative logics and geometries to test whether structures familiar in ordinary experience are genuinely necessary rather than contingently entrenched.

sections.title: Worldview Method and the Necessity Claim
sections.rationale: This issue governs the passage from unavoidable worldview assumptions to the motion-level conclusion that a specifically Orthodox presupposition is necessary, including the distinction between practical reasoning and ultimate justification.

sections.title: Induction, Natural Regularity, and Providence
sections.rationale: Induction is expressly named in the motion, and the central clash concerns whether providence supplies a meta-level justification for scientific regularity or merely relocates an assumption shared by competing accounts.

sections.title: Logic, Reductio, and Preconditions of Discourse
sections.rationale: This issue tests the operative transcendental method through non-contradiction, reductio, meaningful assertion, and alternative logics, determining whether denial of familiar logical principles undermines argument itself.

sections.title: Abstract Content and Orthodox Metaphysical Grounding
sections.rationale: The debate's claim of specifically Orthodox necessity depends materially on whether Platonist alternatives can explain abstract objects and whether the logoi and essence-energies account resolves shared conceptual content and participation.

sections.title: Actual Experience, Modality, and Alternative Systems
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether structures found in ordinary experience support logical or metaphysical necessity when non-classical systems remain conceivable, and how an experience-based formulation connects to the asserted modal conclusion.

routes.description: Establish that Christian teachings about sin, forgiveness, suffering, judgment, social regulation, and human equality form a morally coherent account whose difficult texts can be reconciled with its governing ideals.
routes.successCriteria: Show how Christianity grounds forgiveness and hope, gives a coherent account of suffering and judgment, and distinguishes enduring moral commitments from context-specific legal or congregational accommodations concerning slavery and women.

motionBridge.description: Christianity withstands the motion-level objections if its central moral claims remain coherent after the skeptical challenges are addressed.

centralBridges.description: Connect human wrongdoing, Christ's sacrifice, forgiveness, judgment, resurrection, and restoration within one account of divine justice and grace.
Explain why Christian hope and divine participation in suffering need not be reduced to psychological consolation or evasion of evil.
Distinguish divine moral ideals from temporary regulation or locally directed restrictions in contested biblical passages.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how transcendent commitments can support meaning and well-being beyond self-directed secular individualism.
Relate contextual readings of disputed rules to broader Christian commitments concerning human equality and participation.

routes.description: Establish that Christianity's consoling functions and contested portrayals of divine conduct, slavery, and gender hierarchy create unresolved evidential and moral objections to its claims about forgiveness, judgment, and moral authority.
routes.successCriteria: Show that alternative explanations weaken appeals to Christianity's benefits and that specific biblical teachings or omissions resist accommodation-based defenses strongly enough to challenge the claimed coherence of divine goodness and moral authority.

motionBridge.description: Christianity fails the motion-level test if its account leaves substantial skeptical objections to truth, divine character, or scriptural morality unresolved.

centralBridges.description: Separate Christianity's psychological or social usefulness from evidence that its consoling and salvific claims are true.
Test whether portrayals of suffering, divine speech, anger, and judgment are consistent with the asserted moral character of God.
Determine whether biblical slavery provisions merely regulate existing practices or morally authorize avoidable ownership, mistreatment, and family separation.
Determine whether New Testament restrictions concerning women are local measures or evidence of a broader subordinating moral framework.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply technological and social explanations for modern anxiety that compete with explanations centered on religious decline.
Test whether statements of spiritual unity entail corresponding changes to earthly institutions and social distinctions.

sections.title: Meaning, Well-Being, and the Truth of Consoling Belief
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether religion's association with meaning or well-being supports Christianity's claims, whether secular individualism explains existential distress, and whether consolation instead supplies a non-truth-based explanation for belief.

sections.title: Sin, Suffering, Forgiveness, and Divine Judgment
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on the Christian account of human rebellion, Christ's suffering, forgiveness, resurrection, and final restoration, as well as the objection that biblical responses to suffering portray divine authority as frightening rather than morally reassuring.

sections.title: Slavery, Legal Accommodation, and Moral Endorsement
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether biblical slavery laws are temporary regulations within a fallen society or forms of moral permission, including whether avoidable rules on ownership, punishment, and family separation undermine the accommodation distinction.

sections.title: Spiritual Equality, Women, and Contextual Restrictions
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether New Testament equality language and contextual interpretation can reconcile restrictions involving enslaved people and women with Christianity's claimed moral ideals and social implications.

routes.description: Establish that contingent existence, religious experience, or moral obligation provides a defensible inference to an objective transcendent ground identifiable with God.
routes.successCriteria: At least one affirmative line must connect the relevant experience or fact to a necessary, objective, and non-arbitrary divine ground while answering the principal non-theistic alternative.

motionBridge.description: Show that at least one of the three proposed domains warrants affirming God's existence rather than merely describing human thought or feeling.

centralBridges.description: Connect experienced contingent beings and their totality to an external sufficient reason that does not itself require a further explanation.
Show that the character of religious experience is better explained by an objective transcendent cause than by a wholly subjective account.
Connect objective moral obligation and the authority of moral law to a transcendent ground of value that is neither arbitrary nor socially contingent.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish an experiential inference to a necessary being from an a priori attempt to define that being into existence.
Explain how moral disagreement and culturally variable precepts remain open to criticism by reference to an objective ideal order.

routes.description: Show that the contingency, religious-experience, and moral-obligation arguments do not require God because their key inferences are invalid, underdetermined, or matched by non-theistic explanations.
routes.successCriteria: Prevent each affirmative line from reaching its divine conclusion by challenging its central inference or supplying an adequate account that does not presuppose a transcendent being.

motionBridge.description: Show that none of the proposed domains supplies sufficient grounds for moving from observed experience or practice to God's existence.

centralBridges.description: Challenge the application of necessity to beings and the inference from explanations of particular contingent things to an explanation of their totality.
Show that private experiences and their beneficial effects cannot discriminate an external divine object from subjective or incompatible interpretations.
Account for moral discrimination and obligation through feeling, custom, education, or imagined social disapproval without invoking divine authority.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require that claims about a being whose essence includes existence avoid treating existence as a predicate or reviving an ontological inference.
Use historical and cultural variation in perceived duties to test the asserted universality and absoluteness of moral law.

sections.title: Contingency and the meaning of necessary existence
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether an empirically encountered contingent being can support a coherent modal inference to a being that cannot fail to exist.

sections.title: The totality of contingent beings and sufficient reason
sections.rationale: This issue tests the indispensable move from explanations within the world to an external explanation of the world or totality as such.

sections.title: Religious experience and an objective transcendent cause
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether the distinctive character of mystical awareness supplies grounds for an objective divine reality rather than a subjective event.

sections.title: Competing reports and transformative effects
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether conviction, beneficial transformation, and experiential veracity can distinguish divine contact from incompatible or fictional objects.

sections.title: Moral feeling, objective value, and critical standards
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether moral distinctions require an objective standard and whether identifying goodness with a divine source establishes rather than assumes God.

sections.title: Moral obligation, variation, and its explanatory ground
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the authoritative sense of obligation requires a transcendent lawgiver or is adequately explained by historical customs, education, and social disapproval.
